summary.text:
A large unitary with an unusually strong cash position and an unusually complicated set of things it has invested in. At 30 June 2026 it held £709.1m of investments and owed £350.3m, so on the face of it this is a council with money rather than a council with debt. The picture underneath is more interesting than that.

Not all of the £709.1m is the council's own. £169.3m belongs to other bodies whose cash North Yorkshire holds — the fire and rescue authority, three national parks, the pension fund, and above all the York and North Yorkshire Combined Authority, whose balance nearly doubled during the quarter from £65.3m to £120.3m. The council's own cash is £539.8m. The investment return of 4.19% beat every SONIA benchmark, including the 12-month rate of 4.01%, which is a genuinely good result.

The debt is cheap, long and static: £340.3m of PWLB at 3.72% and £10m of market loans at 4.15%, with no new borrowing taken in the quarter and none forecast. The 2026/27 borrowing requirement is negative £16.4m — the council expects to repay more than it raises. Two thirds of the debt matures beyond twenty years. Financing costs take 2.84% of the non-HRA net revenue stream and 11.55% of the HRA's, both comfortable.

That comfort is bought by £225.8m of under-borrowing against a capital financing requirement of £704.3m. The council has chosen to fund capital from its own cash rather than borrow, which the report is explicit about as a value-for-money judgement and equally explicit is "not risk free". At current PWLB rates that judgement is saving a great deal of money.

The area that repays attention is the £109.8m of alternative investments yielding 6.26%. £70.1m of that is lent to the council's own companies at rates from 3.75% to 10.25%, including £26.1m to Brierley at 9.75% and £31.6m to Broadacres Housing Association at 4.27%. £13.9m sits in three property funds which have returned £3.07m of income but lost £1.64m of capital, down 11.8% since purchase. And three commercial properties are all worth less than was paid: Harrogate Royal Baths is down 34.7% and yielding 1.59%, Scarborough Travelodge down 11.1% at 7.84%, a Co-op store down 22.0% at 6.00%. A fourth, a bank unit in Stafford, was sold during the quarter for £285,000 — a £591,000 capital loss against having earned £716,800 of revenue since 2018-19.

None of this is distress. The council sets money aside against these losses, says so, and has stopped buying assets for yield. But it is where the questions are.

21027.summary:
Executive is asked to note the Q1 treasury position and refer it to Audit Committee. The headline performance is strong: 4.19% on investments against a top SONIA benchmark of 4.01%, no new borrowing, no breach of any indicator, and a borrowing requirement for the year that is negative.

The questions are all in the alternative-investment tables at paragraphs 3.26 to 3.35, which is also where the report is least forthcoming. Three commercial properties are carried below cost, one was sold at a loss during the quarter, and £70.1m is out on loan to council-owned companies at rates that in one case reach 10.25%.

Two small things are also worth a correction. The recommendation at 3.36 asks members to note activity "during the second quarter", when this is Q1. And the Total Other Alternative Investments row shows a return of 2.43% while its only component, Commercial Investments at £25.8m, shows 5.43%.

questions.q: Harrogate Royal Baths is carried at £6.205m against £9.504m invested — down 34.7% — and is forecast to return 1.59%. The council's own debt costs 3.74%. On what basis is holding it better than selling it?
questions.why: This is the clearest case in the portfolio of an asset yielding less than the cost of the money that supports it. The report notes the loss and the return separately, and never puts them next to each other.

questions.q: The Stafford bank unit sold for £285,000 against a £591,000 capital loss, having generated £716,800 of revenue since 2018-19. Once financing costs over those eight years are included, did the council make or lose money on it?
questions.why: The report presents the revenue and the capital loss as if they roughly offset. They only do so if the money tied up in the asset was free, and it was not.

questions.q: £26.1m is lent to Brierley at 9.75% and £3.5m to NY Highways at 10.25%. What security sits behind those loans, and is the interest being received in cash or rolled up into the balance?
questions.why: A 9.75% rate on a loan to a company you own is priced for real risk. Whether the interest is actually being paid is the difference between a good return and a growing exposure.

questions.q: The Combined Authority's balance held by this council rose from £65.3m to £120.3m in one quarter, and is now 17% of the total. What notice can it give to withdraw, and what would that do to our investment maturity profile?
questions.why: £169.3m of the £709.1m belongs to other bodies. Cash you hold for someone else can leave on their timetable, not yours.

questions.q: The rate forecast in the report is dated 25 March. Long PWLB rates are higher now than the 30 June figures in the report's own table. Does the negative £16.4m borrowing requirement still hold, and what is the plan for the £225.8m of under-borrowing?
questions.why: The strategy of using internal cash instead of borrowing looks better the higher rates go, so the answer may be reassuring. But £225.8m is a large position to run on a forecast approaching five months old.

questions.q: The three property funds have lost 11.8% of capital while returning 22.1% in income since purchase. What is the exit plan, and what has been set aside against the £1.637m unrealised loss?
questions.why: Paragraph 3.29 says funds will be set aside so there is no General Fund impact until units are sold. The amount actually set aside is not stated.

email.subject: Your Executive meeting on 18 August — six questions on the treasury report
email.body:
Dear Councillor,

Your Executive meets on Tuesday 18 August and the Q1 treasury management report is on the agenda. We track council treasury papers and PWLB borrowing rates, and we have read it. The council's own performance in it is strong, so this is not a complaint — it is the set of questions we would want answered if we were in the room.

What the report shows. The council held £709.1m of investments at 30 June, earning 4.19% — better than every SONIA benchmark, including the 12-month rate of 4.01%. It took no new borrowing in the quarter, forecasts none for the year, and its borrowing requirement for 2026/27 is negative £16.4m. Financing costs take 2.84% of the General Fund's net revenue stream. On the core treasury numbers this is one of the better positions we have looked at.

The questions are all in the alternative investments section, paragraphs 3.26 to 3.35.

1. Harrogate Royal Baths is carried at £6.205m against £9.504m invested — down 34.7% — and is forecast to return 1.59%. The council's own debt costs 3.74%. On what basis is holding it better than selling it?

2. The Stafford bank unit was sold in the quarter for £285,000, a £591,000 capital loss, having earned £716,800 of revenue since it was bought in 2018-19. Once eight years of financing cost is counted, did the council make or lose money on that asset?

3. £26.1m is lent to Brierley at 9.75% and £3.5m to NY Highways at 10.25%. What security sits behind those loans, and is the interest being paid in cash or rolled up?

4. The Combined Authority's cash held by this council rose from £65.3m to £120.3m in one quarter and is now 17% of the total. What notice can it give to withdraw it?

5. The rate forecast in the report is dated 25 March, and long PWLB rates are higher now than the 30 June figures in the report's own table. Does the negative borrowing requirement still hold, and what is the plan for the £225.8m of under-borrowing?

6. The three property funds have lost 11.8% of capital while returning 22.1% in income. What has actually been set aside against the £1.637m unrealised loss?

We would press question 1. It is the one place in the portfolio where an asset is plainly earning less than the money supporting it costs, and the report reports the two facts several pages apart.

Two small corrections, offered helpfully rather than as gotchas: the recommendation at 3.36 asks you to note activity "during the second quarter" when this is Q1, and the Total Other Alternative Investments row shows 2.43% where its only component shows 5.43%.

Every figure above is from the Executive's own paper and we are happy to send page references.

If it is useful, PWLBtoday runs short courses for councillors on reading treasury reports and on what the prudential indicators mean in practice — written for members, not for accountants. Details are at pwlbtoday.org, and you are welcome to ask us a question either way.

With best wishes,

PWLBtoday
pwlbtoday.org
